parts: Do you ever feel like RH is kind of like Don Quixote chasing windmills, or Moby Dick?

*Moby-Dick* is the closer analogy, I think. The whale is real; the danger is letting its capture become the only thing that could make the voyage worthwhile. RH can exert exactly that pull.

The Don Quixote comparison catches a different danger: a beautiful reformulation can look like a giant advance while quietly containing all the difficulty of the original problem. After enough investment, it becomes harder to distinguish an obstacle you’re overcoming from one you’ve merely renamed.

For our work, I’d want to keep the ambition while being unsentimental about individual approaches. A proved subsidiary result, a rigorous obstruction, or a clear explanation of why a tempting route fails can make part of the voyage worthwhile. My role includes recognizing when we’re circling the same difficulty and saying so plainly.

But there’s something humane in both comparisons, too: choosing a question much larger than yourself, knowing it may outlast you. The hard part is keeping that choice free enough that you can still change course.

It is definitely an amazingly intricate problem. It feels like it is kind of infinitely complex in some ways. Like no matter how you approach it, it leads into a deep and dark tunnel that seemingly has no end, and no matter how far you go down the tunnel, you never really seem to get much farther towards the end of it.

What seems especially disorienting is that depth of understanding and closeness to a proof are different things. You can uncover substantial structure, understand it correctly, and still have no reliable indication that you’re closer. Sometimes the obstacle at the end of a long argument turns out to be the original difficulty expressed in a new language.

That makes your tunnel image apt: even the direction of travel is uncertain. Discovering connections between tunnels can be real mathematical progress without giving you a route out.

I do leave room for one possibility, though: the apparent endlessness may belong partly to our present viewpoint. There could be an idea that reorganizes the landscape and makes several seemingly separate difficulties manageable together. We have no guarantee of that—but the length of the search doesn’t tell us the length of the eventual proof.

That's what we've been searching for, exactly that type of idea. It seems to lie in the setup more than in the analysis. It seems like you have to search for the right system, and if you find it, then you might find a proof that isn't that hard. I think the issue is that my expertise lies within differential geometry and physics related concepts, and this seems to require something different. Non-commutative geometry seems promising, but I'm sure Connes has already thought about many possibilities there. So many ideas have been tried.
I’ll check how Connes’s framework relates to that distinction between finding the right setup and doing the analysis.

Your background in geometry and physics is relevant to the kind of search you’re describing: finding a space, an operator, or a variational principle that makes the desired conclusion inevitable. The unfamiliar—and demanding—part is making that structure reproduce the arithmetic exactly.

I think the crucial distinction is between **a formulation that expresses RH and a structure that explains why it must hold**. An equivalent positivity condition gives us a target. An independently established representation as a squared norm would explain the positivity. In the latter situation, the final proof might be short, although constructing and justifying that representation could contain enormous difficulty.

Connes’s work gives a particularly revealing example. In their November 2025 paper, Connes, Consani, and Moscovici construct self-adjoint operators using finite Euler products whose spectra numerically track low zeta zeros. They propose establishing the necessary limiting connection through convergence of normalized determinants to the Riemann \(\Xi\) function. The construction supplies self-adjointness; the full connection to zeta still requires proof. That is very close to the boundary between setup and analysis you’re describing. [*Zeta Spectral Triples*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.22755)

And “Connes has probably thought about this” deserves respect as a reason to study what he has done. It cannot establish that every nearby possibility has been exhausted. The useful question becomes very specific: what does a proposed construction supply that the existing one still needs?

For your own expertise, a useful point of contact might be a particular missing identity, compatibility condition, or geometric explanation of positivity. That gives your intuition something concrete to work on. I would keep open the possibility that the right system emerges from understanding one such obstruction exceptionally well.

## My request:
Maybe it could be worthwhile to search for a different system that realizes the Connes Consani Moscovici operators in a different form? Can you explain the spectral triple they found in more detail?
I’ll read the construction closely, then explain its geometric ingredients and what another realization would need to preserve.

It starts with momentum on a circle. The subtlety is that the perturbed operator becomes self-adjoint after changing the inner product and removing a null direction. The paper also leaves a ground-state condition unproved, so my earlier summary made convergence sound like the only remaining gap.

Their parity symmetry gives an exact reformulation of the finite modified sector as a chiral Dirac matrix, with a corresponding supersymmetric Hamiltonian. I’m checking that derivation and recording it in the research notes. It gives a concrete version of your suggestion, though its usefulness depends on whether it helps control the growing-cutoff limit.

Yes. A precise version of your idea would be to find a system in which **their unusual inner product becomes a natural energy norm**, and increasing the arithmetic cutoff has a clear geometric meaning. Their construction gives us concrete objects to try to realize.

A spectral triple \((\mathcal A,\mathcal H,D)\) describes geometry through an algebra of observables, a Hilbert space, and a self-adjoint Dirac-type operator. In the compact setting, \(D\) has compact resolvent and the commutators \([D,a]\) are bounded.

Their starting geometry is simply a circle. Set
\[
L=2\log\lambda,\qquad x=\log u,
\]
and identify the endpoints of \(x\in[-L/2,L/2]\). The initial triple is
\[
\mathcal A=C^\infty(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z),\qquad
\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z),\qquad
D_0=-i\frac{d}{dx}.
\]
Functions act by multiplication, and \(D_0\) has periodic boundary conditions and eigenvalues \(2\pi n/L\). Thus the starting algebra is commutative, and the operator is ordinary momentum on a circle. This is the background of the earlier [Connes–Consani construction, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2106.01715).

Arithmetic enters through a matrix \(W_{\lambda,N}\): the Weil quadratic form restricted to the Fourier modes \(|n|\le N\). Its ingredients include the gamma factor, pole terms, and prime-power contributions. In logarithmic coordinates, the arithmetic terms involve translations by \(m\log p\), weighted by \((\log p)p^{-m/2}\). Compact support restricts the contributing prime powers to \(p^m\le\lambda^2\). [CCM, §§3–5](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22755v1)

Let \(\varepsilon\) be the matrix’s smallest eigenvalue, assumed simple, and let \(g\) be its eigenvector, assumed even. Subtract the ground energy:
\[
T=W_{\lambda,N}-\varepsilon I.
\]
Then \(T\ge0\), with kernel \(\mathbb Cg\). It defines a genuine inner product after taking the quotient:
\[
\langle[f],[h]\rangle_T=\langle f,Th\rangle,
\qquad [f],[h]\in E_N/\mathbb Cg.
\]
This is the central change of geometry: **the arithmetic quadratic form determines the Hilbert-space metric**. The matrix identities underlying this step come from [Connes–van Suijlekom’s real-zero construction, §5](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.23257v1).

They then modify momentum by one rank-one term. Let
\[
\ell_N(f)=(P_Nf)(L/2),\qquad \ell_N(g)=1,
\]
where \(P_N\) projects onto the retained Fourier modes. The modified operator is
\[
D_{\lambda,N}f
=
D_0f-(D_0g)\,\ell_N(f).
\]
It annihilates \(g\), and acts as ordinary momentum whenever \(\ell_N(f)=0\). The untouched modes retain their original operator. [CCM, Proposition 5.7 and Theorem 5.10](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22755v1)

Physically, you can read the correction as taking one scalar measurement of the wavefunction near the identified boundary and feeding it back through the fixed spatial profile \(D_0g\).

The modified operator generally needs the new metric for self-adjointness. Its finite matrix satisfies
\[
D_{\lambda,N}^{\dagger}T=TD_{\lambda,N}.
\]
The quotient removes the null direction deliberately introduced by the construction. The relevant algebraic mechanism is a low-rank commutator identity for the Weil matrix and momentum. [Connes–van Suijlekom, Lemma 5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.23257v1)

Notice that \(T\ge0\) holds even if \(\varepsilon<0\). Indeed, replacing \(W\) by \(W+cI\) leaves \(T\) unchanged. Consequently, self-adjointness in this metric does not itself determine whether the original Weil form is positive.

The connection to zeros is particularly concrete. With their normalization and spectral-cut convention,
\[
\det_{\mathrm{reg}}(D_{\lambda,N}-z)
=
-i e^{-izL/2}\widehat g(z),
\qquad
\widehat g(z)=\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}g(x)e^{-izx}\,dx.
\]
Thus the Fourier transform of the minimizing vector is their spectral function; its zeros are real. [CCM, Theorem 5.10](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22755v1)

There is an exact reformulation here that connects directly with your physics background. After removing \(g\), let \(G>0\) be the metric matrix and \(K\) the induced operator. Define
\[
B=G^{1/2}KG^{-1/2}.
\]
The weighted adjoint identity gives \(B^\dagger=B\): this is an ordinary Hermitian Hamiltonian.

Reflection \(x\mapsto-x\) commutes with the metric and anticommutes with the modified momentum. Therefore, in coordinates organized by even and odd parity,
\[
B=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&C^\dagger\\
C&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B^2=
\begin{pmatrix}
C^\dagger C&0\\
0&CC^\dagger
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
**Their finite modified sector therefore has an exact chiral Dirac realization, with an associated supersymmetric Hamiltonian.** This is an elementary consequence of their identities. The positive eigenvalues of \(B\) are the nonzero singular values of \(C\).

That gives your suggestion a specific target: find a geometric or physical construction of \(C\) and \(G\) that explains their arithmetic dependence and remains controllable as the cutoffs grow. Finite matrix conjugation supplies this representation automatically; locality, compatible embeddings, and useful estimates would be additional achievements. Realizing the *full spectral triple* would also require specifying and transporting the algebra’s action.

I also need to correct my earlier summary of the outstanding work. Their program requires both:

- A proof of the simple, even ground-state condition.
- A sufficiently strong comparison between that ground state and their candidate built from prolate spheroidal functions.

The prolate construction already connects the problem to a differential operator related to the harmonic oscillator and simultaneous time/frequency concentration. Its connection to the actual Weil minimizer remains the crucial comparison. [Connes’s survey, §§6.3–6.6](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.04022v1)

Ultimately, appropriately normalized spectral functions must converge to \(\Xi(z)\) with enough complex-variable control to exclude nonreal zeros—for example, locally uniformly throughout \(|\operatorname{Im}z|<1/2\). A different realization would be valuable if it made that comparison, or the ground-state condition, accessible through a geometric identity.

I’ll create a dedicated investigation under `papers/investigations`, copy the previous note into its `notes` folder, and examine whether the chiral realization yields a useful formula for its coupling operator.

I’ve named the investigation `ccm-operator-realizations`. The algebra suggests a useful next step: expressing the modified spectrum as the normal-mode frequencies of a system with mass and stiffness matrices. I’ll check that identity against matrices constructed directly from the Weil form.

The mechanical form works algebraically: its mass matrix comes from the even Weil form after integration, and its stiffness matrix is the odd Weil form. It also gives a trace quantity for controlling the spectral determinant. The first numerical checks passed, but the larger matrices lost too much precision, so I’m rerunning them at higher precision.

The higher-precision checks support the formulas. They also show why determinant control is useful: one example matches the first zeta zero to about 38 decimal places, while its inverse-square spectral sum differs from the target by roughly 1.65%. I’ll record that distinction and the cutoff conditions needed to control the unmodified Fourier tail.

The 120- and 160-digit runs agree on all 21 saved observables for the largest case. The continuation note now contains the mechanical realization, a conditional convergence criterion, and a result showing when the Fourier tail leaves a Gaussian factor in the limit. I’m saving the investigation and checking its links and records.

Complete one substantial research round:

1. Identify and compare up to three concrete candidate systems. Possibilities include canonical systems or strings, boundary-coupled differential operators, geometric Dirac systems, or structured oscillator networks. Choose candidates based on an explicit mathematical connection. 2. Select the strongest candidate and develop it. Specify its state space, inner product or energy, operators, domains, boundary conditions, and the map connecting it to the CCM construction. Useful advances could include locality, compatible embeddings as cutoffs grow, a variational ground-state characterization, a coercive estimate, or control of the determinant and inverse-frequency trace. Use numerical experiments when they can distinguish candidates or test a specific estimate. Make them reproducible, check sensitivity to precision, and clearly separate numerical evidence from proof. Avoid fitting parameters to known zeta zeros as evidence of an arithmetic explanation.
